analysis.one_liner: Bars the US government from putting American citizens on assassination lists without due process.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on a bill to prohibit the government's extrajudicial killing of US citizens; it died in committee after two months with no action beyond a subcommittee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for anyone in the US government, including the President, to order or conspire to the extrajudicial killing of an American citizen — that is, killing a citizen deliberately without a trial, without the citizen directly fighting in a war zone, and without a self-defense justification. It also would have required the President to tell the congressional intelligence committees within 7 days which American citizens are on CIA or military 'kill or capture' lists, and to certify that no citizens are being added. The bill was a response to reports that US citizens had been placed on CIA and military targeted-killing lists.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American citizen gains a legal barrier against being deliberately killed by their own government without a trial or judicial review. The bill's findings singled out Anwar al-Awlaki, a US citizen publicly placed on a CIA target list, as the kind of case this would cover [S3]. Congressional intelligence committees would also gain a mandated window into the identities of citizens on killing lists [S2].

how_it_helps.text: No one, including the President, may instruct a government employee or agent to engage in or conspire in the extrajudicial killing of a US citizen [S3].

The bill leaves legal uses of force intact: killing after a trial with due process, force against a citizen directly participating in hostilities in an active war zone, and ordinary law-enforcement uses like self-defense and freeing hostages [S2].

Within 7 days of enactment, the President must give the congressional intelligence committees a report identifying every US citizen on CIA or Joint Special Operations Command 'high value target' lists, plus written assurance that no citizens are being added [S2].
The bill states Congress's view that no citizen can be deprived of life without due process and that post-9/11 military authorization is not limitless [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The executive branch loses unilateral discretion to place citizens on kill lists without telling Congress; private contractors acting on behalf of the government would also be bound by the prohibition [S3].

drawbacks.text: The prohibition excludes lethal force against a citizen 'directly participating in hostilities' in an active war zone, so much of the actual battlefield use of force would be unaffected [S2].

Enforcement depends on disclosure: the bill relies on presidential reports and assurances to intelligence committees, which get classified briefings and have limited means to verify or act on them [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the practical objection: intelligence officials argue that in counterterrorism operations against people outside any functioning court system, a due-process requirement may be impossible to satisfy and could tie the government's hands against citizens actively plotting attacks — the very case the White House made for targeting al-Awlaki, as described in the bill's own findings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is strong and directly aimed at a real, documented practice: US citizens on government kill lists with no trial and no judicial review. The main weaknesses are that the war-zone exemption swallows much of the field and that the oversight mechanism is essentially trust-based disclosure to committees. On balance it would have created a meaningful legal check on a power the executive branch had begun exercising with none.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, got one routine subcommittee referral, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on July 30, 2010, joined by six Democratic cosponsors [S1, S4, S5].
The Speaker referred it the same day to three committees — Intelligence (Permanent Select), Judiciary, and Armed Services — for consideration of provisions in each committee's jurisdiction [S5].
On September 20, 2010, the House Judiciary Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch came out ahead: it kept, without any congressional check, the authority to place American citizens on targeted-killing lists and to use lethal force against them without a trial or judicial review. The congressional intelligence committees likewise avoided any new obligation to be told who is on those lists.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting extrajudicial killing of US citizens and requiring disclosure of citizens on CIA and military kill lists

for.name: 6 of 253 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Conyers, Filner, Grijalva, Stark, Ellison, and Jackson of Illinois)

against.name: House committee chairs (Intelligence, Judiciary, Armed Services)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral, 111th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill; it stayed at the subcommittee referral stage until the Congress ended

against.name: The Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Maintained the targeted-killing policy the bill sought to prohibit, including the public placement of US citizen Anwar al-Awlaki on a CIA kill or capture list

sides.party_line_note: There was never a floor vote, so no party split is recorded; the sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled committees that buried it were of the same party as the Democratic administration whose policy the bill targeted.

industries.note: The bill's findings cite reporting that contractor Blackwater/Xe was involved in CIA and JSOC targeted-killing programs [S3], and the prohibition covers any 'agent acting on behalf of the United States Government', which would have foreclosed contractors' role in lethal targeting of citizens.

industries.industry: Intelligence and military agencies (CIA, Joint Special Operations Command)
industries.note: The bill would have criminalized ordering the extrajudicial killing of US citizens and forced the agencies to disclose which citizens are on their kill lists, ending a practice they had conducted without disclosure [S2, S3].
